config.title: Build typed column definitions with renderers

intro.title: Build typed column definitions with renderers
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a set of typed column definitions for a data table using TypeScript. You will learn how to define a type-safe structure for columns, including properties like a unique key, a header label, and a custom render function. The core concept is using TypeScript generics and interfaces to create reusable, type-safe components that can render different data types correctly. You'll work with TypeScript's type system to ensure your renderer functions receive the correct data shape. By the end, you'll have a functional column definition system that enforces types at compile time.
intro.usecase: Typed column definitions with renderers are essential for building data-rich interfaces like admin dashboards, financial reporting tools, and e-commerce analytics panels. In products like Salesforce, Shopify Analytics, or internal admin portals, developers use this pattern to display tabular data with consistent formatting, interactive cells, and conditional styling. For example, a customer support dashboard might render priority tickets with colored badges, format currency values consistently, and make email addresses clickable links—all through typed column renderers. This approach ensures type safety while allowing flexible UI customization for different data types and business rules.

objectives: Construct a typed column definition interface for a data table
Implement type-safe renderer functions for different data formats
Configure column definitions with specific renderer assignments
Initialize a typed columns array with proper TypeScript annotations
Apply the typed column definitions to render a structured table
Manipulate renderer logic to conditionally format displayed values
Integrate custom renderers with existing column definition structures

steps.title: Import React and TypeScript utilities
steps.instruction: Import React from 'react' and import the 'ColumnDef' type from '@tanstack/react-table'.
steps.hint: Use import statements at the top of your file. The ColumnDef type will help define typed columns later.
steps.seedCode:

steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the necessary imports to start building typed column definitions.
successCriteria: React is imported from 'react' and ColumnDef is imported from '@tanstack/react-table'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported both React and the ColumnDef type as specified.

steps.title: Define the data type interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'Product' with properties: id (number), name (string), price (number), and inStock (boolean).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Product interface is defined with the correct properties and types, ready to be used for typed column definitions.
successCriteria: The Product interface exists with id: number, name: string, price: number, and inStock: boolean properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check that all four properties (id, name, price, inStock) are included with the correct types (number, string, number, boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The Product interface is missing or incorrect. Make sure to define an interface with all required properties and their types.

steps.title: Define the column definition interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named ColumnDefInterface that describes a column definition with key, header, and an optional renderer property.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword to define the structure. The renderer should be optional (use '?').
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a typed interface that can be used to create column definitions with consistent structure.
successCriteria: An interface named ColumnDefInterface is defined with required key and header properties and an optional renderer property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your interface has all required properties: key, header, and optional renderer.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword and include key, header, and optional renderer properties.

steps.title: Create sample data array
steps.instruction: Create a sample data array named 'sampleData' that contains at least 3 product objects matching the Product interface you defined earlier.
steps.hint: Define a constant array with objects that have id, name, category, price, and inStock properties. Use the correct types from your Product interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a typed array of product data that can be used with your column definitions.
successCriteria: A constant array named 'sampleData' exists with at least 3 objects that match the Product interface structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an array, but check that all objects match the Product interface exactly (id, name, category, price, inStock).
steps.feedbackWrong: The sample data array is missing or doesn't match the Product interface. Create an array with objects that have all the required properties.

steps.title: Create typed column definitions array
steps.instruction: Create a typed array named 'columns' that contains column definition objects using the ColumnDefInterface interface. Define at least three columns for id, name, and price.
steps.hint: Use the ColumnDefInterface type to ensure each object has the required header and accessorKey properties matching the Product interface keys.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed array 'columns' is created with at least three column definition objects, each having header and accessorKey properties that match the Product interface.
successCriteria: The 'columns' array is defined with the ColumnDefInterface[] type and contains objects for id, name, and price columns.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the column definitions, but make sure the array is typed as ColumnDefInterface[] and includes at least id, name, and price columns.
steps.feedbackWrong: The column definitions array is missing or incorrect. Ensure you create a typed array named 'columns' with proper column objects.

steps.title: Define a basic renderer function
steps.instruction: Create a typed function named 'renderPrice' that takes a number parameter 'value' and returns a JSX element showing the value formatted as currency (e.g., '$' + value.toFixed(2)).
steps.hint: Define a function with proper TypeScript typing for the parameter and return type. Use JSX to return a <span> with the formatted value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed renderer function 'renderPrice' is defined, taking a number and returning a JSX element with formatted currency.
successCriteria: The function 'renderPrice' is defined with a typed parameter and returns JSX with proper formatting.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the function is named 'renderPrice', takes a number parameter, and returns JSX with the formatted value (e.g., '$' + value.toFixed(2)).
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition is missing or incorrect. Create a function named 'renderPrice' that accepts a number and returns a JSX element showing the value as currency.

steps.title: Add renderer to column definitions
steps.instruction: Update the price column definition in your column definitions array to use the formatPrice renderer function you created earlier.
steps.hint: Add a 'cell' property to the price column object and assign it the formatPrice function. The cell property should be a function that takes the cell context and returns the formatted value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The price column definition now includes a cell renderer that formats prices with a dollar sign and two decimal places.
successCriteria: The price column object has a 'cell' property
The cell property is assigned the formatPrice function
The formatPrice function is called with the cell context
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're adding the 'cell' property to the price column object and assigning it the formatPrice function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to modify the price column definition in the columnDefinitions array to include a cell property that uses the formatPrice function.

steps.title: Create the main component structure
steps.instruction: Create a React functional component named ProductTable that returns a simple wrapper div element.
steps.hint: Define a component using either function declaration or arrow function syntax, with proper TypeScript typing for a functional component.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ProductTable functional component is defined with a return statement that outputs a div wrapper.
successCriteria: The ProductTable component is created with proper TypeScript typing and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the component, but make sure it's named ProductTable and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you defined a functional component named ProductTable that returns a div.

steps.title: Implement table rendering logic
steps.instruction: Inside the ProductTable component, implement the table rendering logic by mapping over columnDefinitions to generate table headers and sampleData to generate table rows.
steps.hint: Use the columnDefinitions array to create <th> elements for headers and the sampleData array to create <tr> elements with <td> cells for each column.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ProductTable component will have the structure to render table headers from columnDefinitions and table rows from sampleData.
successCriteria: The component maps over columnDefinitions to create <th> elements and maps over sampleData to create <tr> elements with <td> cells for each column.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the table rendering, but make sure to map over both columnDefinitions for headers and sampleData for rows.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're mapping over columnDefinitions to generate table headers and sampleData to generate table rows inside the ProductTable component.

steps.title: Apply renderers in table cells
steps.instruction: In the ProductTable component's tbody section, modify the cell rendering to use the renderer function from the column definition when it exists, otherwise display the raw cell value.
steps.hint: Check if the column definition has a 'cell' property (the renderer function) and call it with the cell data if available.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: conditional renderer usage
const cellValue = column.cell ? column.cell({ cell: { getValue: () => data[column.accessorKey] } }) : data[column.accessorKey];
steps.expectedOutcome: The table cells will display formatted prices (e.g., "$999.99") for the price column while other columns show raw values.
successCriteria: The tbody cell rendering checks for column.cell
The formatPrice renderer is called for price cells
Other cells display the raw product property value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're checking if the column has a 'cell' property and calling it with the appropriate cell data when available.
steps.feedbackWrong: The table cells aren't using the renderer functions correctly. Review how to conditionally apply the renderer from the column definition.
